claims.claim: Taha Yasseri compared 1,800 matched article pairs and found Grokipedia averages about 14,200 words against 9,400 on Wikipedia.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, Trinity College Dublin, arXiv:2510.26899v2
claims.quote: Grokipedia articles average about 14,200 words versus 9,400 on Wikipedia
claims.modelEra: Grok, October-November 2025; register measured: encyclopedic articles — the archival register the program wanted

claims.claim: Yasseri measured a mean Flesch-Kincaid grade of 19.3 for Grokipedia against 12.8 for Wikipedia across 1,811 matched pairs.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, Trinity College Dublin, arXiv:2510.26899v2
claims.quote: indicating more syntactically complex and less reader-friendly prose
claims.modelEra: Grok, autumn 2025; register measured: encyclopedic articles

claims.claim: Yasseri measured 21.4 references per thousand words on Grokipedia against 90.2 on Wikipedia, and 2.87 headings per thousand words against 5.58.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, Trinity College Dublin, arXiv:2510.26899v2
claims.quote: longer but less lexically diverse articles, with fewer references per word
claims.modelEra: Grok, autumn 2025; register measured: encyclopedic articles

claims.claim: Yasseri's measured lexical diversity gap is very small: type-token ratio 0.244 on Grokipedia against 0.248 on Wikipedia, a difference of 0.004 at p equals 0.02.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, Trinity College Dublin, arXiv:2510.26899v2
claims.quote: inflates sentence length and readability grade without a proportional increase in lexical variety
claims.polarity: asserts (and qualifies the abstract's 'less lexically diverse' summary, whose measured gap is 0.004)
claims.modelEra: Grok, autumn 2025; register measured: encyclopedic articles

claims.claim: Yasseri concludes that AI-generated encyclopedic content mirrors Wikipedia's informational scope but diverges in editorial norms, favouring narrative expansion over citation-based verification.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, Trinity College Dublin, arXiv:2510.26899v2
claims.quote: favoring narrative expansion over citation-based verification
claims.modelEra: Grok, autumn 2025; register measured: encyclopedic articles

claims.claim: Neil Clarke asserts that generative AI use differs from plagiarism in that proving it to a legal standard is significantly more complex, since few leave a prompt in or admit what they did.
claims.quote: proving it to a legal standard is significantly more complex
claims.page: body, on why editors should not name names
claims.modelEra: July 2026; models unnamed; register measured: short-fiction submissions

claims.claim: Clarke states that a handful of publishers are willing to publish generated slop and that at minimum they should be transparent about it.
claims.quote: There are a handful of publishers that are ok with generated slop.
claims.page: final bullet, 'YOU MAY DISCOVER THEY DO NOT CARE'
